Reliability in DMAR: Choosing the Coefficient, Choosing the Interval

Ken Kelley

November 2026

Source: vignettes/reliability.Rmd
reliability.Rmd
library(DMAR)

Reporting the reliability of a composite score involves two separable decisions, following the framework of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016): choosing the coefficient and choosing the interval.

  • Choosing the coefficient. The coefficient reported is a claim about the measurement model and about which composite is scored. Each coefficient below estimates the proportion of composite variance attributable to the common factor, under different commitments about the model. Choosing a coefficient is choosing which commitments the analysis makes.
  • Choosing the interval. Given the coefficient, the confidence interval method is an empirical performance question: which procedures cover the population value at their nominal rate across realistic conditions. The Monte Carlo studies of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) addressed that question, and the DMAR defaults encode their recommendations.

The map for choosing the coefficient:

Function The composite The claim being made
reliability_alpha() unit-weighted sum one factor with equal loadings (essential tau-equivalence)
reliability_kr20() sum of 0/1 items alpha’s claim, for binary items
reliability_omega() (robust omega, the default) unit-weighted sum one congeneric factor for the numerator only; the composite variance is estimated from the data
reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied") unit-weighted sum one congeneric factor; the fitted model reproduces the composite variance
reliability_omega_categorical() sum of observed ordinal categories a probit threshold model links items to one factor for the numerator only; the total variance comes from the unrestricted polychoric correlations
reliability_omega_categorical(denominator = "model_implied") sum of observed ordinal categories a probit threshold model links items to one factor; the fitted model reproduces the polychoric correlations (Green & Yang, 2009)
reliability_H() optimally weighted composite one congeneric factor; a different composite, not a different assumption

The vignette walks the table top to bottom on one running example, then turns to the interval.

A Running Example

A six-item congeneric scale with unequal loadings, which is the normal state of real items:

set.seed(113)
N <- 300
lambda <- c(0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8)
eta <- rnorm(N)
items <- sweep(matrix(rep(eta, 6), N, 6), 2, lambda, `*`) +
  matrix(rnorm(N * 6), N, 6) %*% diag(sqrt(1 - lambda^2))
colnames(items) <- paste0("y", seq_len(6))

Alpha Assumes Equal Loadings

Coefficient alpha equals the population reliability when the items are essentially tau-equivalent, that is, when every item loads equally on the common factor. When loadings differ, alpha underestimates. On the running example the loadings range from .4 to .8, so alpha sits a little below omega:

res_alpha <- reliability_alpha(data = items, ci_method = "none")
res_omega <- reliability_omega(data = items,
                               denominator = "model_implied",
                               ci_method = "none")
c(alpha = res_alpha$value[res_alpha$term == "estimate"],
  omega = res_omega$value[res_omega$term == "estimate"])
#>     alpha     omega 
#> 0.7976157 0.8067366

The gap here is modest because the loadings, though unequal, are of similar magnitude. The gap grows when the tau-equivalence assumption fails badly, and with real tests a common way for it to fail is in how the composite is scored rather than in the tests themselves. Four of the tests in the Holzinger and Swineford (1939) data (holzinger_swineford) measure spatial ability: visual perception, cubes, paper form board, and lozenges. Because the tests are scored on different scales, their raw-score loadings on a common factor are far from equal, and the unit-weighted sum of the raw scores, the composite alpha and omega describe here, carries that inequality. cfa_1() fits the single factor with the loadings free, the congeneric model behind omega, and with the loadings constrained to be equal, the essentially tau-equivalent model behind alpha:

spatial <- holzinger_swineford[, c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes",
                                   "t3_paper_form_board", "t4_lozenges")]
d_spatial <- descriptives(spatial)$descriptives
print(d_spatial[, c("variable", "mean", "sd")], digits = 3)
#>               variable mean   sd
#> 1 t1_visual_perception 29.6 7.00
#> 2             t2_cubes 24.4 4.71
#> 3  t3_paper_form_board 14.2 2.83
#> 4          t4_lozenges 18.0 9.05
congeneric <- cfa_1(data = spatial)
congeneric[startsWith(congeneric$term, "lambda") |
             congeneric$term %in% c("chi_square", "df"),
           c("syntax", "term", "estimate")]
syntax term estimate
f1 =~ t1_visual_perception lambda_f1_1 4.728
f1 =~ t2_cubes lambda_f1_2 2.240
f1 =~ t3_paper_form_board lambda_f1_3 1.427
f1 =~ t4_lozenges lambda_f1_4 5.898
chi_square 1.855
df 2 
tau_equivalent <- cfa_1(data = spatial, equal_loading = TRUE)
tau_equivalent[tau_equivalent$term %in% c("chi_square", "df"),
               c("term", "estimate")]
term estimate
chi_square 69.658
df 5 
a_spatial <- reliability_alpha(data = spatial, ci_method = "none")
o_spatial <- reliability_omega(data = spatial,
                               denominator = "model_implied",
                               ci_method = "none")
est_spatial <- c(alpha = a_spatial$value[a_spatial$term == "estimate"],
                 omega = o_spatial$value[o_spatial$term == "estimate"])
est_spatial
#>     alpha     omega 
#> 0.6220163 0.6794339

The standard deviations of the four tests run from 2.83 (paper form board) to 9.05 (lozenges), and the raw-score loadings follow them. The congeneric model reproduces the covariances of the four tests closely, and constraining the loadings to be equal does not. For the sum of the raw scores, alpha falls 0.057 below omega, against 0.009 on the running example, so alpha here answers under an assumption this composite violates.

Tau-equivalence is a property of the composite as scored, not of the tests alone. Standardizing each test before summing gives every test the same variance and makes a different composite, the sum of the z-scores:

spatial_z <- as.data.frame(scale(spatial))
congeneric_z <- cfa_1(data = spatial_z)
congeneric_z[startsWith(congeneric_z$term, "lambda"),
             c("syntax", "term", "estimate")]
syntax term estimate
f1 =~ t1_visual_perception lambda_f1_1 0.675
f1 =~ t2_cubes lambda_f1_2 0.476
f1 =~ t3_paper_form_board lambda_f1_3 0.504
f1 =~ t4_lozenges lambda_f1_4 0.652 
a_z <- reliability_alpha(data = spatial_z, ci_method = "none")
o_z <- reliability_omega(data = spatial_z,
                         denominator = "model_implied",
                         ci_method = "none")
est_z <- c(alpha = a_z$value[a_z$term == "estimate"],
           omega = o_z$value[o_z$term == "estimate"])
est_z
#>     alpha     omega 
#> 0.6643619 0.6695794

The standardized loadings run from .476 to .675, a narrower spread than the running example’s .4 to .8, and on this composite alpha falls only 0.005 below omega. The sum of the raw scores and the sum of the standardized scores are different composites with different reliabilities, and a reported coefficient is a claim about the composite actually scored. The pattern generalizes: each coefficient is correct under its stated model, and the choice among them is a choice among models.

A Hypothetical Example: Items With Widely Unequal Loadings

On the standardized spatial tests the gap all but closed, because their standardized loadings differ little. Items with equal variances can still differ widely in how strongly they reflect the factor, and then alpha falls well below omega. The items here are hypothetical, constructed to show the point: six items, each with population variance 1, three loading .9 on the factor and three loading .1, as in a scale where half of the items barely track the construct. The population alpha and omega follow from the loadings:

lambda_hyp <- c(0.9, 0.9, 0.9, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1)
k_hyp <- length(lambda_hyp)
Sigma_hyp <- tcrossprod(lambda_hyp) + diag(1 - lambda_hyp^2)
# Alpha from the item variances and the variance of the sum; omega as
# the share of the variance of the sum that the factor accounts for.
pop_hyp <- c(alpha = k_hyp / (k_hyp - 1) *
               (1 - sum(diag(Sigma_hyp)) / sum(Sigma_hyp)),
             omega = sum(lambda_hyp)^2 / sum(Sigma_hyp))
pop_hyp
#>     alpha     omega 
#> 0.6258373 0.7177033

Then 300 respondents are drawn from this population, and both coefficients are estimated as before. The draws reuse the running example’s seed, so the factor scores and the normal deviates behind the errors are those of the running example, and only the loadings differ:

# withr::with_seed() restores the generator state afterward, so drawing
# these items does not change the random numbers the later examples use.
N_hyp <- 300
items_hyp <- withr::with_seed(113, {
  eta_hyp <- rnorm(N_hyp)
  sweep(matrix(rep(eta_hyp, k_hyp), N_hyp, k_hyp), 2, lambda_hyp, `*`) +
    matrix(rnorm(N_hyp * k_hyp), N_hyp, k_hyp) %*%
    diag(sqrt(1 - lambda_hyp^2))
})
colnames(items_hyp) <- paste0("y", seq_len(k_hyp))
a_hyp <- reliability_alpha(data = items_hyp, ci_method = "none")
o_hyp <- reliability_omega(data = items_hyp,
                           denominator = "model_implied",
                           ci_method = "none")
est_hyp <- c(alpha = a_hyp$value[a_hyp$term == "estimate"],
             omega = o_hyp$value[o_hyp$term == "estimate"])
est_hyp
#>     alpha     omega 
#> 0.6516687 0.7383066

In the population, alpha falls 0.092 below omega, and in the sample, 0.087, against 0.057 for the sum of the raw spatial scores and 0.009 on the running example, whose six items also have variance 1. These items already share one variance, so standardizing them leaves the gap in place: alpha falls below omega because the equal loadings it assumes are far from the loadings that generated the items.

The Denominator Choice in Omega

Coefficient omega requires an estimate of the composite’s total variance in its denominator, and reliability_omega() offers two. The default, denominator = "observed" (robust omega), estimates the composite variance directly from the data, which is consistent for the actual variance of the scale score whether or not the one-factor model is right. The alternative, denominator = "model_implied", uses the total variance reproduced by the fitted single-factor model, which is correct exactly when the one-factor model reproduces the composite variance.

The coefficient was built for the following situation. Model misfit is treated as a set of minor common factors, visible as residual correlations: the scale is then not perfectly unidimensional, but a single-factor approximation is retained. The coefficient isolates the variance attributable to the general factor only, excluding the minor factors, and expresses it relative to the observed variance of the unweighted composite. Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) named it hierarchical omega after that hierarchical factor logic; upon reflection, we would have named it observed omega or robust omega, and DMAR uses robust omega. Two qualifications keep the name accurate. The robustness is to misspecification of the total variance only, because the numerator remains model based under either denominator; and robust omega is distinct both from outlier-robust estimation of alpha and omega (Zhang & Yuan, 2016) and from the robust maximum-likelihood standard errors available through ci_method.

When the one-factor model holds, the two agree, as on the running example:

o_mi <- reliability_omega(data = items,
                          denominator = "model_implied",
                          ci_method = "none")
o_ob <- reliability_omega(data = items, ci_method = "none")
c(model_implied = o_mi$value[o_mi$term == "estimate"],
  observed      = o_ob$value[o_ob$term == "estimate"])
#> model_implied      observed 
#>     0.8067366     0.8056993

Now contaminate the scale with a nuisance doublet, a shared specific factor on the first two items, the sort of minor structure real item sets carry:

doublet <- rnorm(N)
items_d <- items
items_d[, 1] <- items[, 1] + 0.6 * doublet
items_d[, 2] <- items[, 2] + 0.6 * doublet

o_mi_d <- reliability_omega(data = items_d,
                            denominator = "model_implied",
                            ci_method = "none")
o_ob_d <- reliability_omega(data = items_d, ci_method = "none")
c(model_implied = o_mi_d$value[o_mi_d$term == "estimate"],
  observed      = o_ob_d$value[o_ob_d$term == "estimate"])
#> model_implied      observed 
#>     0.7846721     0.7693093

The two now diverge, and only robust omega still answers the question a reliability coefficient is supposed to answer, the proportion of the variance of the composite you actually computed that is attributable to the common factor. The divergence itself is diagnostic: a nontrivial gap between the two denominators says the one-factor model is not reproducing the composite variance, and the right response to a large gap is to model the structure, not to choose a denominator. Note also what the observed denominator does not fix: the fitted loadings absorb part of the doublet under either setting, so checking the one-factor model (for example with cfa_1()) remains part of reporting any omega.

A small gap is not evidence of the reverse. A doublet or a method factor shared by a few same-signed items inflates their loadings while leaving the two denominators close, so the gap cannot certify the numerator. The residual correlations of the single-factor fit are the more direct check, and every omega carries them: the printed table names the denominator and the largest residual correlation, and the full matrix is in the residual_cor attribute.

o_ob_d
term value
estimate 0.769
se NA
ci_lower NA
ci_upper NA
conf_level 0.950
N 300
N_complete 300
n_items 6

Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega)

Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.228 (y1 with y2)

attr(o_ob_d, "residual_cor")$items
#> [1] "y1" "y2"

Here the largest residual sits on the doublet pair. The residuals detect local dependence more reliably than they locate it: when the shared variance sits on the items that dominate the factor, the single factor absorbs it and the misfit appears among the other items.

Categorical Omega for Ordered Items

When items are ordered categories (Likert responses, symptom counts), the composite people score is a sum of those observed categories, and the category thresholds make the item-factor relationship nonlinear. Categorical omega (Green & Yang, 2009) fits the probit threshold model and returns the reliability of the categorical sum score on its own metric. The threshold configuration decides how much this matters relative to treating the items as continuous. First the benign case, every item cut at the same thresholds:

items_same <- apply(items, 2, function(x)
  as.integer(cut(x, breaks = c(-Inf, -1, -0.2, 0.6, Inf))))
colnames(items_same) <- colnames(items)

oc_same <- reliability_omega_categorical(data = items_same, ci_method = "none")
o_same  <- reliability_omega(data = items_same, ci_method = "none")
c(categorical_omega     = oc_same$value[oc_same$term == "estimate"],
  treated_as_continuous = o_same$value[o_same$term == "estimate"])
#>     categorical_omega treated_as_continuous 
#>             0.7820753             0.7755024

With similar threshold patterns across items the two approaches nearly agree, which is precisely the condition under which Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016, Study 3) found the continuous treatment held its interval coverage. In real item sets the threshold patterns typically differ across items: some items skew one way, some the other. Cutting the same underlying responses with threshold patterns that differ across items:

breaks_hi <- c(-Inf,  0.5,  1.2,  1.9, Inf)
breaks_lo <- c(-Inf, -1.9, -1.2, -0.5, Inf)
breaks_by_item <- list(breaks_hi, breaks_hi, breaks_hi,
                       breaks_lo, breaks_lo, breaks_lo)
items_cat <- sapply(seq_len(6), function(j)
  as.integer(cut(items[, j], breaks = breaks_by_item[[j]])))
colnames(items_cat) <- colnames(items)

oc <- reliability_omega_categorical(data = items_cat, ci_method = "none")
o_as_cont <- reliability_omega(data = items_cat, ci_method = "none")
c(categorical_omega     = oc$value[oc$term == "estimate"],
  treated_as_continuous = o_as_cont$value[o_as_cont$term == "estimate"])
#>     categorical_omega treated_as_continuous 
#>             0.7190046             0.6755575

The two now diverge, here by about 0.04, with the continuous treatment understating on this configuration. The direction and size of the continuous treatment’s error depend on the threshold configuration, which is exactly what makes it untrustworthy as a general practice; in Study 3 its interval coverage failed as threshold patterns diverged across items. Categorical omega is constructed on the metric of the summed categories themselves, so it is the coefficient to report for ordinal items, which is why reliability() routes integer-coded, few-category items to reliability_omega_categorical() automatically.

Categorical omega and robust omega share a design principle in Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016): in both, the total variance in the denominator is not taken from the fitted factor model. Robust omega estimates it from the sample covariances; categorical omega, as computed there and by default here, assembles it from the unrestricted polychoric correlations and the thresholds. In each case the fitted single factor supplies only the numerator, so the coefficient stays anchored to the composite that is actually scored even when the factor model is an approximation.

Green and Yang (2009) defined their coefficient with the other denominator. Their appendix program takes “the reproduced (model-based) correlation matrix” as the input to the denominator, so the original categorical omega is the model implied version, and correlated errors enter its total variance only when they are specified in the model. denominator = "model_implied" reproduces it:

oc_mi <- reliability_omega_categorical(data = items_cat,
                                       ci_method = "none",
                                       denominator = "model_implied")
c(unrestricted  = oc$value[oc$term == "estimate"],
  model_implied = oc_mi$value[oc_mi$term == "estimate"])
#>  unrestricted model_implied 
#>     0.7190046     0.7171456

With a single factor generating these items the two nearly agree, as the continuous pair did on the running example; they part ways as the model misfits, and the residual polychoric correlations in the residual_cor attribute show where.

The unrestricted denominator asks more of the data than the model implied one. Every unrestricted polychoric correlation must be estimable, and when two items are skewed in opposite directions their bivariate table can have empty cells that leave the correlation without a finite standard error: every respondent below the top category of one item sits in the bottom category of the other. In Green and Yang’s own mixed-skew design (two items piled into the top category, two into the bottom), most samples of 500 have such a pair. The default then stops with an error naming the pair rather than filling the correlation with an arbitrary value, and denominator = "model_implied" remains available, since the fitted model gives that correlation no weight and supplies its own value for it. It does so only while the correlations the data do determine identify the loadings, which takes a link from every item to the others, directly or through other items, and at least one cycle of an odd number of items (three items whose three correlations are all determined, for example). When every correlation between the two top-piled items and the two bottom-piled ones is undetermined, the determined ones fix only the products of the loadings within each pair: the relative sign of the pairs is free, and the fit can return loadings of opposite signs and a categorical omega near 0.05 against a population value of 0.716. Both denominators then stop with an error naming the pairs and the unlinked blocks of items. A bootstrap of the default meets the problem more often still: the few respondents in the sparse cells are what determine the correlation, and a resample often leaves some of them out, so in Green and Yang’s design at a sample size of 1,000 about half the replications of a bootstrap of the default are set aside even when the sample itself determines every correlation. The printed bootstrap line and a warning count them, and the model implied denominator keeps all but those whose remaining correlations leave the loadings unidentified or whose solution is improper: 1 of 200 in a bootstrap of the help page’s complete data, of 1,000 respondents, but a median of 42% in samples of 300 from the same design. When fewer than half of the replications return a value, no interval is reported, since the rest would be a minority of the resamples, chosen by whether they returned one; a larger sample is the remedy. The help page of reliability_omega_categorical() works through that design.

Coefficient H: A Different Composite

Coefficient H (Hancock & Mueller, 2001) makes the same congeneric claim as omega but changes the composite: it is the reliability of the optimally weighted combination of the items, the best possible composite the items can form, rather than the unit-weighted sum. The two coincide when loadings are equal and diverge as loadings spread, because optimal weights exploit the stronger items:

res_H <- reliability_H(data = items)
res_H
term value
estimate 0.847
se 0.014
ci_lower 0.817
ci_upper 0.873
conf_level 0.950
N 300
N_complete 300
n_items 6 
c(omega = res_omega$value[res_omega$term == "estimate"],
  H     = res_H$value[res_H$term == "estimate"])
#>     omega         H 
#> 0.8067366 0.8472086

From raw data, reliability_H() fits the single-factor model exactly as reliability_omega() does, and its interval is a Wald interval on the logit scale whose standard error comes from the delta method over the full covariance matrix of that fit’s parameter estimates, robust maximum likelihood by default, as for omega. When the factor belongs to a larger confirmatory or structural model, pass the fitted model instead, reliability_H(fit, factor = "..."), and the standard error is the one that model was fitted with. The form reliability_H(loadings = , se_loadings = ) is not used here. It builds the interval from the marginal standard errors of the standardized loadings, which leave out the covariances among the loading estimates; those estimates are correlated in any fitted factor model, so its interval can be too narrow or too wide, and every such call gives a warning saying so.

Report omega when people will score the scale by summing; report H when scores will come from the factor model itself (or to see the ceiling the item set could reach with optimal weighting). Reporting both, with one sentence on which composite each describes, is often the most informative choice under unequal loadings. Read H as a ceiling, too, in the statistical sense: the sample H overestimates the population coefficient, and a composite formed with weights estimated from the sample is less reliable than H says, both markedly in samples of about 100 and barely beyond about 1,000 (Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, & McIntosh, 2019). A bootstrap interval for H (ci_method = "bca", as for omega) also estimates that bias. Reliability coefficients matter because researchers score and use composites; an analysis conducted entirely within the SEM framework, relating latent variables directly, has less need of them.

KR-20 completes the family as the binary-item special case of alpha, provided for the classical test theory literature that names it separately; reliability_kr20() and reliability_alpha() agree on 0/1 data.

Choosing the Interval

Choosing the interval is an empirical question, and it is the subject of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016): across coefficients, sample sizes, loading patterns, distributions, and (for categorical items) threshold patterns, which interval procedures cover at their nominal rate. The DMAR defaults are their recommendations, with one refinement for omega described below the table:

Coefficient Default behavior Recommended interval and basis
alpha Bonett (2002) interval well behaved among the closed forms under normality
omega, model implied Wald interval with the robust ML standard error, its limits formed on the logit scale ("mlr_logistic") the best performing closed form when item distributions deviate from normality; the limits are formed on the logit scale on the evidence of a later study
robust omega point estimate; a message names the bootstrap call percentile or BCa bootstrap, the pairing recommended when unidimensionality is approximate; no closed form exists for the observed denominator
categorical omega point estimate; a message names the bootstrap call BCa bootstrap, which held coverage across threshold patterns, category counts, and sample sizes

The logit form for omega comes from a Monte Carlo study run for DMAR (in the package’s source repository, methodology/reliability_limits), which compared the two forms of the Wald limits from the same standard error: the normal theory maximum likelihood one for normal data and the Huber-White one of MLR for nonnormal data. With normal data the limits on the scale of omega missed mostly on one side, the population value falling below the lower limit, and covered from .910 to .952; formed on the logit scale and transformed back (Browne, 1982; Kelley, 2007), they covered from .939 to .956 in every cell. With complete data the default takes lavaan’s robust.sem standard error, which no cell used; it estimates the same asymptotic variance as the Huber-White one. fa_confirmatory() forms the limits of its omega row on the logit scale too. ci_method = "mlr" forms the limits on the scale of omega. The examples below name the default, ci_method = "mlr_logistic", where they use it; leaving it out gives the same interval.

Coefficient H was not among the coefficients Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) compared. Its default is omega’s: a Wald interval on the logit scale with the robust ML standard error, the fast choice, with the percentile or BCa bootstrap the safer one for a reported analysis.

A bootstrap is never run unless it is requested. When one is requested, B = 10000 replications is the default.

Every reliability function offers its interval methods through ci_method (Feldt, Fisher, Bonett, Hakstian-Whalen, ML, robust ML, ADF, their logistic transformed variants, and the bootstrap family, as applicable). Except for coefficient H, the default is the method with simulation evidence behind it. Two practical notes. The bootstrap methods need raw data, not a covariance matrix, and take a seed argument for reproducibility. And a bootstrap interval on the categorical coefficient refits an ordinal factor model per replicate, so it is the slowest interval in the family; the default B = 10000 is a deliberate accuracy choice, worth the wait for a final analysis and worth reducing while exploring.

# The default: robust omega, point estimate, with the message naming
# the bootstrap call.
reliability_omega(data = items)
#> Robust omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "percentile" (or "bca"); B = 10000 replications is the default when you do.
term value
estimate 0.806
se NA
ci_lower NA
ci_upper NA
conf_level 0.950
N 300
N_complete 300
n_items 6

Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega)

Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.096 (y1 with y3)


# The recommended interval, requested explicitly (B reduced here to
# keep the vignette fast; the default is B = 10000).
reliability_omega(data = items, ci_method = "percentile",
                  B = 500, seed = 113)

Missing Data: FIML and Auxiliary Variables

The mlmr() vignette makes the case at length: listwise deletion is unbiased only when values are missing completely at random, and it is inefficient always. The same argument applies to a reliability analysis, so reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() (and the reliability() wrapper) take the same position mlmr() does. Two arguments govern the treatment:

  • missing = c("fiml", "listwise", "two_stage"). The default, "fiml", keeps every case with at least one observed item, or with an auxiliary variable observed, and estimates by full information maximum likelihood, consistent and efficient under the weaker missing at random (MAR) assumption; "listwise" analyzes the complete cases alone. Data in which no value is missing are analyzed as they stand, with the same estimates FIML would give and the complete data intervals, so the default analysis is FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise. fa_confirmatory() differs: it fits complete data by FIML too. The complete data analysis is used here because the closed-form intervals of alpha and omega (Bonett’s among them) need it. Without auxiliary variables a row with every item missing does not count as a missing value, since listwise deletion and FIML both drop it. With auxiliary variables, a case whose items are all missing still informs the item moments through its auxiliaries, and setting it aside would make the analysis conditional on having an observed item, which biases the estimates when the items go missing together at random given the auxiliaries.
  • aux, a character vector naming auxiliary variables: columns of data that are not part of the composite but are correlated with the items or with the reasons values are missing. They enter as saturated correlates (Graham, 2003): correlated freely with each other and with every item’s residual, never loading on the factor and never entering the composite. The measurement model is undisturbed while FIML uses their information, and missingness that depends on the auxiliary becomes MAR once the auxiliary is conditioned on (Collins, Schafer, & Kam, 2001). Supplying aux implies missing = "fiml".
# Missingness on y2 that depends on an auxiliary z (MAR given z):
# listwise deletion is biased here, FIML with z is not.
z <- eta + rnorm(N, sd = 0.5)
d <- data.frame(items, z = z)
d$y2[runif(N) < plogis(-1 + 1.5 * as.numeric(scale(z)))] <- NA

# Listwise, asked for by name: the analysis drops the incomplete rows.
reliability_alpha(data = d[, paste0("y", 1:6)], missing = "listwise")
term value
estimate 0.762
se 0.025
se_transformed 0.106
ci_lower 0.707
ci_upper 0.807
conf_level 0.950
N 215
N_complete 215
n_items 6 

# FIML with the auxiliary: every case with an observed item or an
# observed z contributes, and z informs the estimation.
reliability_alpha(data = d, aux = "z")
term value
estimate 0.796
se 0.019
ci_lower 0.759
ci_upper 0.833
conf_level 0.950
N 300
N_complete 215
n_items 6

The returned table always reports both N (the cases used) and N_complete (the complete cases), so the cost of listwise deletion is legible at a glance. The classical (analytic) alpha under FIML is still the classical coefficient: the same formula, applied to the FIML estimate of the item covariance matrix rather than the complete-case one. Interval methods that cannot be made correct under FIML (the complete-data closed forms, ADF, the profile likelihood) are refused with an explanation rather than silently reverting to listwise deletion; the delta method ("ml", "mlr") and bootstrap intervals remain available. Users of MBESS may recognize the aux idea from ci.reliability(), whose implementation no longer runs on current semTools; DMAR implements the saturated correlates model directly.

Interval Availability and the Reported Denominator

Bootstrap intervals require at least half of attempted replications and at least two defined estimates; AVE also retains a minimum of 100. A point estimate and counts remain available when an interval is withheld. These rules describe estimability and selection among resamples, not a guarantee of coverage. Defined improper values are retained under the stated policy and counted separately.

For categorical omega with multiple imputation, the default is 20 completed datasets inside each bootstrap replication. The point estimate has a separate adaptive rule that uses at least 20. More inner imputations reduce imputation noise at additional computational cost; the default of 20 does not rest on a calibration of coverage. A fraction of missing information estimated from a selected minority of replications is explicitly qualified and cannot certify precision merely by increasing the point’s number of imputations.

A planning sensitivity result takes the probability of obtaining an interval within the target width, the mean width, and the coverage over one denominator, the simulated studies that returned an interval. A study that returns no interval is in none of them; the output states how many studies were attempted, how many returned an interval, and how many did not, and its simulation attribute gives Monte Carlo limits for the width-target probability.

One Entry Point and the Broom Verbs

reliability() dispatches on type (or auto-detects: ordered few-category items go to categorical omega, otherwise omega) and forwards denominator and ci_method (here the default of the model implied omega, named); every family member returns the same tidy shape with tidy() and glance() methods:

res <- reliability(data = items, type = "omega",
                   denominator = "model_implied",
                   ci_method = "mlr_logistic")
generics::tidy(res)
#>    term  estimate         se  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level wald_df
#> 1 omega 0.8067366 0.01652757 0.7722706 0.8370868       0.95     Inf
#>   h1_diagnostic wald_calibration_note
#> 1          <NA>                  <NA>
generics::glance(res)
#>   coefficient  estimate         se  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level nobs n_items
#> 1       omega 0.8067366 0.01652757 0.7722706 0.8370868       0.95  300       6
#>      ci_method wald_df h1_diagnostic wald_calibration_note
#> 1 mlr_logistic     Inf          <NA>                  <NA>

Planning the Study

Reliability estimation is also a design problem: a reliability coefficient reported without a narrow interval is a weak claim. ss_aipe_reliability() plans the sample size so the interval for alpha or omega achieves a target width (with an assurance probability if desired), which closes the loop between this family and DMAR’s accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) tradition. It plans for the coefficient this family estimates from the raw item scores, so the population is used as a covariance matrix (a correlation matrix plans for standardized items). Without an assurance the size comes from a closed form for the expected width of the interval type names: the normal theory variance of alpha (van Zyl, Neudecker, & Nel, 2000), evaluated on the population covariance matrix, for the parallel model and for the normal theory interval of the tau equivalent model, and the delta method variance of the model implied coefficient, the variance behind reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml") and reliability_alpha(estimator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"), for the factor analytic interval of the tau equivalent model and for the congeneric model. With an assurance, a Monte Carlo search that starts from that size finds the smallest one whose interval is no wider than the target with the requested probability (Terry & Kelley, 2012); a simulated study whose fit returns no interval counts as one whose interval is too wide.

What Reliability Coefficients Cannot Do

Reliability is a property of a test score in a particular population, not a property of the items in the abstract. A high alpha or omega does not mean:

  • the items measure the construct of interest (that is validity, not reliability);
  • the scale will achieve the same reliability in a different population;
  • averaging across many items has fixed the problem of poor individual item quality.

Single-administration coefficients also book item-specific systematic variance as error, so all of the coefficients here are lower bounds on classical test-retest reliability. Use the family for what it is: an internal-consistency analysis conditional on a substantive theory of what the items mean.
